{{Short description|Topology}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly in the field of [[topology]], the '''K-topology''',{{sfn|Munkres|2000|p=82}} also called '''Smirnov's deleted sequence topology''',{{sfn|Steen|Seebach|1995|loc=Counterexample 64}} is a [[topology (structure)|topology]] on the set '''R''' of real numbers which has some interesting properties. Relative to the [[standard topology]] on '''R''', the set <math>K = \{1/n:n=1,2,\dots\}</math> is not [[closed (topology)|closed]] since it doesn't contain its limit point 0. Relative to the K-topology however, the set ''K'' is declared to be closed by adding more [[open set]]s to the standard topology on '''R'''.  Thus the K-topology on '''R''' is strictly finer than the standard topology on '''R'''.  It is mostly useful for counterexamples in basic topology.  In particular, it provides an example of a [[Hausdorff space]] that is not [[Regular space|regular]].

==Formal definition==

Let '''R''' be the set of real numbers and let <math>K = \{1/n:n=1,2,\dots\}.</math>  The '''K-topology''' on '''R''' is the topology obtained by taking as a [[base (topology)|base]] the collection of all open intervals <math>(a,b)</math> together with all sets of the form <math>(a,b)\setminus K.</math>{{sfn|Munkres|2000|p=82}}
The [[neighborhood (topology)|neighborhood]]s of a point <math>x\ne 0</math> are the same as in the usual Euclidean topology.  The neighborhoods of <math>0</math> are of the form <math>V\setminus K</math>, where <math>V</math> is a neighborhood of <math>0</math> in the usual topology.{{sfn|Willard|2004|loc=Example 14.2}}
The open sets in the K-topology are precisely the sets of the form <math>U\setminus B</math> with <math>U</math> open in the usual Euclidean topology and <math>B\subseteq K.</math>{{sfn|Steen|Seebach|1995|loc=Counterexample 64}}

==Properties==

Throughout this section, ''T'' will denote the K-topology and ('''R''', ''T'') will denote the set of all real numbers with the K-topology as a [[topological space]].

1. The K-topology is strictly finer than the standard topology on '''R'''.  Hence it is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], but not [[Compact space|compact]].

2. The K-topology is not [[Regular space|regular]], because ''K'' is a closed set not containing <math>0</math>, but the set <math>K</math> and the point <math>0</math> have no disjoint neighborhoods.  And as a further consequence, the [[quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] of the K-topology obtained by collapsing ''K'' to a point is not Hausdorff.  This illustrates that a quotient of a Hausdorff space need not be Hausdorff.

3. The K-topology is [[connected (topology)|connected]]. However, it is not [[path connected]]; it has precisely two [[path component]]s: <math>(-\infty, 0]</math> and <math>(0, +\infty).</math>

4. The K-topology is not [[Locally connected space|locally path connected]] at <math>0</math> and not [[Locally connected space|locally connected]] at <math>0</math>.  But it is locally path connected and locally connected everywhere else.

5. The closed interval [0,1] is not compact as a subspace of ('''R''', ''T'') since it is not even [[limit point compact]] (''K'' is an infinite closed discrete subspace of ('''R''', ''T''), hence has no limit point in [0,1]).  More generally, no subspace ''A'' of ('''R''', ''T'') containing ''K'' is compact.
